title: Warren Buffett Speaks With CNBC's Becky Quick — Thursday, March 28

segments.text: So, let's roll the tape and see how that went.

First of all, how did this deal come apart? This comes as a huge surprise to anybody who's been watching this. I know you've had a stake in Burlington Northern, but buying the whole thing, that's a huge deal. $34 billion.

Yeah. Well, a week ago, Thursday, we were the board of directors of Bergkshire was meeting in Fort Worth. We do one off-site meeting a year and we have three subsidiaries in Fort Worth, Justin Boot, and Acme Brick and TTI. So, we pick out a place and go down once a year. And I went down a couple of hours

early last, a week ago, Thursday, and and uh I went over to uh um the NSF and visited with Matt Rose and his top management. permanent home for BNSF uh you know don't forget my phone number and he didn't throw me out of the office. Delighted to be here.

The way that Matt just set this up, he talked about that purchase from nine years ago. Joe pointed out that you did call it a huge bet on the future of the American economy and that bet paid off in a big way. In fact, this year in the annual report, you wrote about BNSF as one of the towering redwoods in the
grove that is Bergkshire Hathway.

So we didn't we didn't coordinate to get our story straight, but it was it was a seinal time for for Bergkshire in either the last days of October, the
early days of November of of of 2009.

And uh uh Matt and I talked at a small hotel uh in Fort Worth and uh our directors are going to meet there in the fall. It'll be the 10th annular. and I've I've just had so much good luck in in Texas, but nothing rivals the uh the BNSF acquisition. One thing you may find interesting, uh I had a talk with Matt

on I guess it was Monday following the Friday I was out here with him and and more or less had the deal and then I called our lawyers and I said, "Uh, you fellows can bill me for all the hours you want between now and Sunday at noon." And after that, you're working for nothing. So I I I we compressed that

deal into a one-wing period or so that otherwise probably would have taken months if I if I hadn't made that made that restriction. Those of you who have dealt on corporate deals will understand why I stuck that in.
I see people taking notes right now. Um we are also looking at Matt retiring next month. He's going to be stepping down. What are you gonna do without him?

Well, he has left us, you know, a great great railroad. It is it is the towering railroad at at Berkshire and and uh we're going to take good care of what he's he's built for us. It is I think I described it, I don't know whether it was in the lead and as being a bet on the country and and and a hundred-year
asset. It's more than a hundred-y year asset, but I thought that would probably be as long as I would be around. So I I didn't want to speak beyond my tenure.

the country. He's he he realizes that it has a significance that goes well beyond that of of virtually any businesses at making sure this country works like the way it we want it to work.
Warren, you've been fascinated with the railroads, I think, since you were a kid.
Right.

Now you look at it as something much more than just a fun toy or or something to kind of aspire to. You watch this as something that's a real way of measuring the economy. You talk all the time about the the car rail loads and I just wonder what you're seeing right now when you look at that statistic what that tells

you about the economy. Yeah, it's distorted in the last week or two by the the floods in the Midwest and we move a lot of coal, but but uh there are 20 odd categories that that the uh rail road industry reports on for all the railroads and winter is always a little bit of a tricky thing, but I would say that it uh

it looks like it's slowing down. I don't mean it's reversed in course or anything but it does it does seem from all of the businesses but especially including railroad statistics because they come so fast uh and they cover such a broad spectrum and it gets distorted by whether people are hurrying up the

Pacific trade because they're worried about tariffs and all of that sort of thing. But I would say that it it does look like uh the pace of increase in the economy has slowed down and I I wouldn't call it call it somewhere close to noticeably but I wouldn't go beyond that.

Have you seen it broadly? Is that when it comes down to commodities when it comes down to things that retailers are ordering when it comes down to energy or are there a couple of areas where you see more weakness? Well, it it there are these 20 odd categories that autos and you know that uh aggregates, you name

you name it. uh grain. uh it most almost all of those categories throughout last year were were u trending strong and and I would say that uh just looking at those figures but also looking at some other figures I good many other figures I see on a on a weekly basis where uh it looks it looks like things have slowed

down and you you'd always have the weather factor but uh uh that's the way I'd bet looking at what I see today I don't want That doesn't change anything we do. I mean, you know, if if there was a flashing red light, if there was a blurring red light, we would keep investing the same way we do. I mean, it

just look at the railroad. We in terms of what the situation was in the fall of 2009. I mean, it it looked like the end of the world and and and and it turned out that that was the low quarter was the third quarter. You really want to bet on America. I mean it uh it uh uh you listen to that magnificent rendition
a few minutes ago and and uh God has blessed America.

Um I I don't want to get too wonky on this but um the yield curve when you look at the 10-year versus the three month has inverted and again this is a pretty important signal. It can signal a recession. It has signaled every recession that we've seen in the last 50 years. And it's only given a an incorrect signal once. It's the first
time it's inverted since 2007. Do you see a recession on the horizon?

Well, though I just hope I see a lot of recessions. I hope I live long enough there. I don't know how many recessions I've lived through, but I was I was born on August 30 of 1930 and the Dow was a little over 250. And it was by the time I got out of college, it hadn't there was only one or two days after my birth

that had been that high. offer us more opportunities but in marketable securities or business if we see a good business and everybody in the world is is is bearish and that that inversion has gone to 100 basis points or something like we're going to buy it and and uh and we'll buy it enthusiastically.

The reason I I kind of push on this though is you've talked an awful lot in the past about how um high yields that you look at act as as gravity on stock prices. So if you're seeing really low yields that inversely could mean that stocks should trade a lot higher. What do you think at this point?

Yeah, the lower interest rates are basically the better the option stocks are because stocks are going to produce whatever they are over the next 20 or 30 or 40 years, but if you buy a 30-year bond, you're going to get that rate or somebody you transfer to. So, when if a 30-year bond is at 2.8 or something or
2.9% and the Federal Reserve's intent now is to have 2% a year inflation, and you pay tax on the 2.8 or 2.9 that you receive.
So your net is down around two. You're essentially saying I'm willing to go with a profitless investment for 30 years. That's never really got my blood.

I don't get excited about that. And and then when you can buy good businesses that may earn 14 15% on tangible equity and they've done it in aggregate for a long long time and you just think of the difference between good businesses and how they'll compound over time. You can start with yields that are

higher than the bond gives you and the the odds that those with a diversified group that that improves over time. It's it's it's a bond with an ascending coupons because that's really all a bond stock is. It's it's a bond with a whole bunch of coupons that go out to infinity and there you just you have to print the

amount on the coupons yourself. You don't know the numbers. But the one thing you know is the numbers on on stocks as a whole are going to be way greater than 2.8%. So, uh, the lower the lower bond yields go, the more attractive stocks are as a long-term investment. And what it says about the next three months or six months or one
year, I don't know. And I really don't care.
All right, let's stick with some of your big Have we lost all the audience now?
Yeah, we're going to change the subject.

I mean once once I'd been once I'd uh lost my virginity essentially. I I thought why stop at one, you know.
Does that mean you like Delta better than the other airlines at this point?
No, I I accidentally went above 10% in.
Yeah, I do that a lot.

I mean it was US Airways went broke a couple of times subsequently and and uh uh I tried to sell our interest at 50 cents on the dollar and couldn't do it. And fortunately it had this period when it

actually did well. So we actually made money on that airline investment. But the the if you look at the number of airlines that went broke in this country, if you look at the number of auto manufacturers that went broke, I mean it it it the capitalism can can be rough. It produces good results overall, but but

Well, I don't think that, you know, obviously Boeing has a lot of work to do very promptly and and and uh the airline industry has been so safe. I mean, unbelievable. the uh we we happen to sell insurance uh also and and the rates uh went down so far just because the the industry is so safe and obviously that

there's a problem with this uh 737 and X and then the uh but Boeing you can bet they're staying up 24 hours a day to get it worked out and that won't change the industry or anything over time but uh uh airline airline tribal And you know it it's it's almost impossible to believe how much that's improved in terms of
safety over the last uh well during my lifetime.
Let's uh stick on the themes. We've already talked about planes and trains.

I think it's a little over, it's around 5% of the company.

can make something, manufacture something there. Again, President Trump has talked to Mary Bar about this. Have you talked to her about it? I've not talked to her. I I haven't seen her for a couple of months. Uh actually, uh we have a lunch date coming up fairly soon.

But I I think Mary Bar has done a sensational job at General Motors. That is not an easy job. And uh now I I am a huge admirer of Mary bar on the job she has done at General Motors. And the auto industry is not a

And and every every footprint that an auto company might have had 50 years ago or 30 years ago or 10 years is going to be obsolete

at some time. and and and the ones they're putting in now are going to be absolutely it's the nature of it. So I they've offered jobs as I understand many of those workers who have are taking them but other plants and and and I capitalism was described as creative destruction and you know we had in we
probably had 15,000 people working at the packing houses many years ago and we don't have them now they work at insurance and frankly I'm glad they are.

Change has been huge in the rail industry. If you look at the safety record and rail, how it's improved and uh you know the efficiency of the operations and that's good for America, good for the shareholders too, but it's good for America. Although the the people get left behind in those situations that
that leads to the political discontent that we've seen in this country.

Well, what you do in a in a country with $65,000 of GDP per capita per capita. That's more than six times what it was when I was born. Here we had a developed economy and now you have six times what we had then. And you do take care of the people that for one reason or another can become, and it's a terrible term to
use, but it's true, rogue in an economy.

with our prosperity, we should take care of people who become in effect roadkill because of something beyond their control. And I'm 100% for free trade. if they've got, you know, the billion, 200 million shares out and it's selling at 35 or something like that, that would be 40 odd billion in the case of GM. mean, that is capitalism. that it's it's produced well just think of what Dallas you know 200 250 years ago three time three lifetimes like mine less than three lifetimes like mine you know there wasn't anything here and just look around you you know as you come from the airport or wherever this is a product of

an incredible system I mean I I get the goosebumps when I hear God Bless America song like that I mean because this this country in three of my lifetimes has turned, you know, something that Lou, you know, the French were willing to sell a quarter of it to us for 15 million bucks.
